row.basis: trembling at the divine word
row.note: The commentary makes inward reverent fear the condition for receiving the reminder; Isaiah says God regards the humble, contrite person who trembles at his word.

row.basis: hearing the Torah to learn fear
row.note: After the command to remind listeners, this assembly is told to hear and learn to fear YHWH, making reception of instruction a cultivated inner response.

row.basis: tender heart hearing the book
row.note: Josiah's heart is tender and he humbles himself when he hears the judgment read; the response depends on the hearer's disposition, as the commentary says the reminder works in the one who fears.

row.basis: those fearing YHWH and a book of remembrance
row.note: Those who fear YHWH speak together, are heard, and have a memorial written before God; this joins the commentary's inward fear to its account of remembering and preserving what might otherwise be lost.

row.basis: memorial stones leading to fear
row.note: The stones recall Israel's crossing so peoples know YHWH's strong hand and Israel fears him always, concretely linking retained memory with reverent fear.

row.basis: remembering the wilderness and testing the heart
row.note: Israel is told to remember the wilderness way because the testing disclosed what was in its heart and whether it would keep the command; recollection and inward orientation meet as in the commentary.

row.basis: children hear and learn to fear
row.note: The children who have not known the Torah are to hear and learn fear of YHWH, showing that the decisive response is acquired by the hearer rather than inherited as a group label.

row.basis: Noah fears concerning what is not yet seen
row.note: Warned about events still unseen, Noah acts in reverent fear and saves his household; this gives a concrete instance of fear before sight prompting a timely response.

row.basis: word held fast in a good heart
row.note: The hearers with an honest, good heart hold the word fast and bear fruit with endurance, closely matching the commentary's claim that the listener, not the messenger, must take the reminder inwardly.

row.basis: the hearer who forgets versus the doer
row.note: James contrasts a hearer who forgets with one who perseveres in the law and acts; it makes explicit the commentary's movement from recovering what slipped away to a changed response.

row.basis: fear of God and doing righteousness in every nation
row.note: Peter says that in every nation the person who fears God and does righteousness is acceptable to him, concretely shifting the criterion from ancestry to the inward posture and conduct emphasized in the commentary.

row.basis: fear, glory, judgment, and worship of the Creator
row.note: The angel commands fear of God and giving him glory because judgment has arrived, then calls for worship of the Creator; this joins reverence to creation and worship as the commentary's surah does.

row.basis: worship with reverence and awe
row.note: The community is to offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe; the next verse grounds this in God as consuming fire, giving the commentary's fear-to-prayer movement a concrete Christian formulation.

row.basis: fear of the one with authority after death
row.note: Jesus redirects fear from human killers to the one who has authority after death, specifying a future, unseen consequence where the Qur'anic verse leaves the object of fear unstated.

row.basis: the Spirit bringing Jesus' words to remembrance
row.note: Jesus promises that the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples of what he said; this parallels the commentary's concern with future recollection while locating its source in divine aid.

row.basis: remembering after the judgment has begun
row.note: Abraham tells the rich man to remember his former life after the chasm is fixed; the memory is real but cannot repair the missed opportunity, like the commentary's late remembrance after Gehenna is brought.

row.basis: recollection after the teacher's departure
row.note: Peter makes provision for his readers to recall his teaching after his death, a specific case of a messenger's reminder becoming the hearer's future act of memory.

row.basis: remembering the prior saying after a reminder
row.note: At the tomb the women remember Jesus' earlier words after the messengers call them to remember; the scene distinguishes the spoken reminder from the hearers' act of recollection.

row.basis: understanding remembered later
row.note: The disciples first fail to understand the events, then remember Jesus' words after his glorification; this supplies a delayed, retrospective counterpart to the commentary's expected near-future remembrance.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary labels the Arabic root ذ ك ر; Deuteronomy uses its Hebrew cognate זכר for remembering YHWH as the giver of Israel's power, recalling dependence rather than crediting oneself.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכרון
row.note: The commentary labels ذ ك ر for remembering; Joshua calls the stones a זכרון, a memorial of the crossing, so a retained sign carries the past forward and leads in verse 24 to fear.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary's Arabic root label is ذ ك ر; the psalm uses Hebrew זכר for remembering God's precepts and doing them, joining memory to enacted obedience.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر; Exodus uses Hebrew זכר of God remembering his covenant and responding to Israel's groaning, a divine answer that contrasts with the hearer's own work of recollection.

row.basis: fear of YHWH as the beginning of knowledge
row.note: Proverbs makes fear of YHWH the beginning of knowledge and contrasts it with despising instruction; this links the commentary's knowledge-laden fear to readiness to receive a reminder.

row.basis: fear and turning from evil as wisdom
row.note: Job identifies fear of the Lord with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding, connecting reverence to both knowing and a changed course.

row.basis: fear placed before Israel to restrain sin
row.note: At Sinai Moses says the divine testing is meant to put fear before Israel so they do not sin; fear is an apprehension of divine presence that shapes what the hearer does.

row.basis: steadfast mercy toward those who fear YHWH
row.note: The psalm describes enduring mercy as belonging to those who fear YHWH, then the next verse describes covenant-keepers who remember his commands; the two verses join inward reverence to active remembrance.

row.basis: serving with fear and trembling
row.note: The rulers are told to serve YHWH with fear and rejoice with trembling, a concrete route from reverence to worship that complements the commentary's later movement toward prayer.

row.basis: forgiveness followed by fear
row.note: The psalm says forgiveness is with God so that he may be feared, reversing the commentary's main order of fear leading to remembrance and showing a distinct scriptural sequence.

row.basis: fear placed in hearts so they will not turn away
row.note: God promises to put fear in the people's hearts to keep them from turning away; this gives the disposition a divine source, sharpening the commentary's account of listener agency within God's will.

row.basis: lips honor while the heart is far away
row.note: Isaiah condemns a fear of God taught as human precept when the heart remains distant, a precise warning against treating outward religious speech as the inward fear that receives the reminder.

row.basis: fear and belief after Israel sees the deliverance
row.note: Israel sees YHWH's great power, then fears and believes; unlike the commentary's person who fears before seeing, this places fear after visible deliverance and makes the difference in timing clear.

row.basis: warning those who forget God
row.note: The psalm warns those who forget God to consider their end before there is no rescuer; it concretizes the commentary's contrast between pursuing what has slipped away and suffering the loss of it.

row.basis: counsel and covenant knowledge for those who fear
row.note: The psalm says YHWH shares his counsel with those who fear him and makes his covenant known to them, linking reverence with knowledge rather than treating fear as uncomprehending panic.

row.basis: conduct in fear before the impartial judge
row.note: Peter tells believers to conduct themselves in fear during their exile because God judges each person's work impartially; the fear is tied to knowledge of a real future reckoning.

row.basis: holiness brought to completion in fear of God
row.note: Paul urges cleansing from defilement and completion of holiness in fear of God, connecting reverence to the purification that the commentary places after remembrance.

row.basis: working out salvation with fear and trembling
row.note: Paul calls the community to act with fear and trembling, then says God is at work in them; this holds human response together with divine action as the commentary does for the listener's open door.

row.basis: fear as the opposite of prideful self-assurance
row.note: Paul says branches were broken off through unbelief and warns the standing branch not to become proud but to fear; this gives a specific counterpart to the commentary's self-sufficient hearer who sees no need to recover anything.

row.basis: fear of punishment cast out by perfected love
row.note: John says fear has to do with punishment and is cast out by perfected love; this distinguishes punitive dread from the commentary's reverential fear instead of making the two senses identical.

row.basis: remembering generations while fearing the Lord
row.note: Ben Sira tells those who fear the Lord to look at generations past and asks who trusted him and was forsaken; remembered precedent supports trust, joining memory and reverence in one argument.

row.basis: fear of sin preceding wisdom
row.note: The Mishnah says wisdom endures when fear of sin precedes it; this directly parallels the commentary's ordering of an inward fear before the act of remembering and receiving instruction.

row.basis: wisdom and fear as reciprocal conditions
row.note: The Mishnah says that without wisdom there is no fear and without fear there is no wisdom, preserving both directions of the relationship that the commentary illustrates with fear leading to remembrance and remembrance sometimes awakening fear.

row.basis: what is in Heaven's hand and fear of Heaven
row.note: The Talmud says all is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven; the commentary, citing the Qur'anic qualification that remembrance depends on God's will, keeps the listener's response inside divine willing, making their accounts of agency diverge.

row.basis: fear of God distinguished from fear of the devil
row.note: Hermas urges fear of God and says this displaces fear of the devil, distinguishing reverent accountability from panic and giving a concrete early Christian account of fear directing conduct.

row.basis: forgetting the God who brought Israel out
row.note: After warning Israel to beware when full and settled, Moses says not to forget YHWH who brought them from Egypt; remembered rescue corrects self-sufficiency and grounds response to instruction.

row.basis: forgetting amid prosperity
row.note: Israel is warned not to forget YHWH by failing to keep his commands when prosperous, a concrete case where a hearer's inner memory determines whether the received teaching governs life.

row.basis: claiming power for oneself
row.note: The imagined heart says its own power made its wealth; this is a specific counterpart to the commentary's self-sufficient hearer who sees no lack and therefore has no reason to seek what was lost.

row.basis: fear expressed in walking, love, and service
row.note: Moses asks what YHWH requires and lists fearing him, walking his ways, loving and serving him, and keeping his commands; fear is an inward posture that issues in a whole course of action.

row.basis: fear known through costly obedience
row.note: The angel says Abraham's fear of God is now known because he did not withhold his son; fear is disclosed by a concrete response, not a group identity or mere claim.

row.basis: fearing YHWH while walking without light
row.note: Isaiah describes the person who fears YHWH, obeys the servant's voice, and walks in darkness without light yet trusts God's name; this concretely joins fear, hearing, and trust before visible resolution.

row.basis: YHWH himself as the one to fear
row.note: Isaiah redirects fear toward the holy Lord of hosts; it supplies an explicit object for the commentary's deliberately uncompleted “whoever fears” and frames awe as response to the transcendent.

row.basis: the Creator's boundary for the sea
row.note: The sea's fixed limit is given as evidence of YHWH's power, followed by the question whether people will fear him; the created order grounds the reverence that the surah's opening creation signs also invite.

row.basis: failure to say in the heart, “let us fear”
row.note: Despite seasonal rain and harvest, the people do not say in their hearts that they should fear YHWH; this locates the missing response inwardly even when signs are present.

row.basis: remembering God's works across generations
row.note: The purpose of teaching the next generation is that they set hope in God, do not forget his works, and keep his commands; this joins transmitted reminder, recovered memory, and action.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر; Psalm 78 uses Hebrew זכר when it says Israel did not remember God's hand or the day he redeemed them, a concrete use of the cognate for lost rescue-history.

row.basis: forgetting the hand that redeemed
row.note: Israel fails to remember a deliverance it experienced and therefore repeats distrust; this adds the commentary's point that forgetting can be a failure to pursue what was once known.

row.basis: children summoned to learn fear
row.note: The speaker calls children to listen and promises to teach them the fear of YHWH, making reverence a learned response to instruction rather than an inherited label.

row.basis: hearers who tremble at the word under pressure
row.note: Isaiah addresses those who tremble at YHWH's word even as their own brothers cast them out; the verse shows reception of the word persisting when the surrounding community rejects them.

row.basis: seeking YHWH with trembling in the latter days
row.note: In the latter days Israel will seek YHWH and David their king and come trembling to YHWH and his goodness; fear is a movement toward seeking, not mere flight.

row.basis: hearing today without hardening the heart
row.note: The quotation warns its hearers that when they hear God's voice they must not harden their hearts; the immediate, personal response to a reminder is the point.

row.basis: the heard message failing to benefit
row.note: The wilderness generation heard good news but it did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith; this makes the commentary's distinction between a reminder passing across and being taken in explicit.

row.basis: reminder of rescue followed by destruction
row.note: Jude says he wants to remind readers who already know that the Lord saved a people from Egypt and later destroyed the unbelieving; memory of rescue becomes a warning about the response that follows.

row.basis: remember, repent, and do the first works
row.note: The church is told to remember its former state, repent, and do its first works, with removal of its lampstand threatened if it does not; recollection must become action while there is time.

row.basis: remembering what was received and heard
row.note: The church is told to remember what it received and heard, keep it, and repent, or the coming will be unexpected; this directly joins received speech, memory, vigilance, and a deadline.

row.basis: remembering endurance after illumination
row.note: Readers are told to remember earlier days after they were enlightened, when they endured public suffering; recollection strengthens present fidelity rather than serving as passive recall.

row.basis: Peter remembers after denying Jesus
row.note: After Peter denies Jesus, the Lord's look makes him remember the prediction, and he weeps bitterly; this gives a precise, painful case of a warning remembered only after failure.

row.basis: mercy to those who fear God through generations
row.note: Mary says God's mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation, carrying the commentary's individual inner quality across time without making it an ethnic class.

row.basis: past events written as warnings for readers
row.note: Paul says Israel's events were written as warnings for those at the end of the ages; this makes scriptural memory a present admonition with consequences, like the commentary's reminder before judgment.

row.basis: command to remember the risen Christ
row.note: Paul directly commands Timothy to remember Jesus Christ raised from the dead; the verse gives a concrete Christian instance of remembered proclamation as the hearer's continuing task.

row.basis: remembering Jesus' words after the resurrection
row.note: After Jesus is raised, the disciples remember his saying about the temple and believe; the delay shows how an event can restore the meaning of a word previously heard.

row.basis: Moses trembling at Sinai
row.note: Hebrews recalls that even Moses said he trembled with fear at the terrifying manifestation; it supplies a concrete bodily response to divine presence alongside the later call to worship with reverent awe.

row.basis: not sharing opponents' fear
row.note: Peter tells believers not to fear what their opponents fear or be troubled; this distinguishes reverence toward God from social intimidation, a useful limit on the commentary's broad language of fear.

row.basis: honoring Christ as holy in the heart
row.note: The next verse directs believers to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts; with 1 Peter 3:14, it specifies where fear and reverence are directed when human pressure is present.

row.basis: fear following visible judgment
row.note: After Ananias and Sapphira die, great fear comes upon the church and all who hear; this is a counter-sequence to fear before sight, showing fear arising after a judgment has become visible.

row.basis: heart closed against hearing and turning
row.note: Jesus cites people whose heart is dull and whose ears and eyes are closed lest they understand, turn, and be healed; this gives a specific account of refusal at the level of perception that blocks a reminder's effect.

row.basis: service without fear after deliverance
row.note: Zechariah speaks of being rescued from enemies so that God's people may serve him without fear; the context makes this freedom from human threat, not the reverent fear of God in the commentary, a meaningful distinction.

row.basis: fear of the Lord as wisdom's beginning
row.note: Ben Sira calls fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom and associates it with the faithful; this places reverence at the start of understanding, complementing the commentary's link between knowing and fear.

row.basis: those fearing the Lord wait for mercy
row.note: Ben Sira tells those who fear the Lord to wait for his mercy and not turn aside; fear sustains a listener through delay rather than being only an immediate fright.

row.basis: fear of God taught as communal conduct
row.note: Clement urges the community to fear the Lord and to teach the young fear of God; this concretely extends the commentary's personal reception of reminder into instruction and conduct across a community.
